title: Louis IX
hookLine: a king who fed the poor at his table, and who also led crusades
carry: a king at table with the poor

lines: A LEPER, OR A MORTAL SIN?
cards: Would you rather be a leper, or commit a mortal sin? A king puts that question to his friend, with others listening.
The friend, a knight named John of Joinville, answers honestly: he'd rather commit a great many sins than be a leper. The king says nothing in front of the others.
Later, alone, he tells Joinville he has it backward: no sickness of the body is as ugly as a sin in the soul. Joinville wrote it all down, years after, in a book about his friend.
The king was Louis, king of France, whom the Church would call a saint: Louis IX.

teach.h: THE POOR AT THE KING'S TABLE.
teach.b: Joinville describes a king who fed the poor, and often had poor men brought to eat where he was, sometimes serving them himself. Louis once asked Joinville whether he washed the feet of the poor on Holy Thursday.
Joinville was horrified: never, he said, the feet of those peasants. Louis told him that was a poor answer, since Christ had done it.
Jesus's words in John, in the Douay-Rheims: "you also ought to wash one another's feet."
Joinville also remembers Louis sitting under an oak tree at Vincennes, hearing anyone who came with a complaint, with no guard between them. There's another side. This same king led crusades.
He was captured in Egypt, ransomed, and died on another crusade in North Africa. The crusades brought war and death to Christians, Muslims and others.
And Louis's laws were harsh to the Jews of France; in his reign copies of the Talmud were burned in Paris.
Catholic historians tell these things too.

teach.h: YOU ALSO OUGHT TO WASH ONE ANOTHER'S FEET.
teach.b: The Church canonized Louis for his faith, his prayer and his charity, not for every decision he made. A saint, Catholics say, is someone in heaven, not someone without faults on earth.
You can admire the king at the table and still name what his wars and laws cost.

how: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Louis, and parishes, cities and schools bear his name; the Church honors him for his faith and charity while historians, including Catholic ones, also examine his crusades and his laws.

games.q: you're Louis. your friend just said, in front of others, that he'd rather sin than be sick. what do you do?
o: rebuke him sharply in front of everyone.
say nothing then, and talk to him alone later.
laugh it off and never mention it.
games.why: Louis waited and corrected him in private, so his friend wasn't shamed. Joinville wrote it down years later.

practice: Choose someone you admire, living or dead: a parent, a teacher, a figure from history.
First see clearly what's good in them, then, without anger, let one real fault come into view, and hold both in the same hand without erasing either. If you pray, pray for them as they really were.

wordCard.voice: Louis IX. The king of France remembered as Saint Louis: a king who fed and served the poor, and who also led crusades. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: to wash. The verb Jesus uses in John 13:14 for washing one another's feet.
